quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

- **No mother is identified** anywhere in the tree

**BCG Standard 11 flag:** Thomas's role as father rests only on household co-residence (indirect evidence) and an un-extracted death certificate. His birth date has no source. This plan prioritizes records that confirm or challenge the assumed relationship before treating it as established.

| # | Type | Place | Year(s) | Repository | Notes |

The plan begins with the **1860 census** (pli_004), already tied to a record in the tree but never formally extracted — its content, including the name of Thomas Flynn's wife, has never been recorded in the research. From there it moves to the **1880 census** (pli_005), the first to state family relationships outright, and then to **Thomas Flynn's probate records** (pli_006), where a will naming Patrick as son would settle the father question definitively. Three additional census years (1870, 1900) fill out the full span of Patrick's life; **naturalization records** are searched to find Thomas's Irish county of origin and unlock future searches in Ireland; **Patrick's own marriage record** is browsed for any statement of his parents' names; and a **FAN sweep** of Irish-born neighbors in the 1860 census closes the plan.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

The 1860 census lists all household members by name, age, sex, occupation, and birthplace; Thomas's wife — Patrick's mother — very likely appears here and would be named for the first time in the evidence record. Collection 1473181 is name-searchable. Surname variants Flyn, Flinn, Flyne should be tried. Note: the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly; co-residence is indirect parentage evidence.

The 1880 census is the first US census to record each person's relationship to the head of household by name. Patrick (~age 35) in Thomas's household would yield a stated parent-child relationship — the strongest census evidence for parentage confirmation. Even if Patrick has his own household by 1880, his entry names his father's and mother's birthplaces, corroborating the Irish origin established in item 1. Thomas's household will also show his wife (Patrick's mother) by name, cross-confirming item 1. Collection 1417683 is name-searchable.

Thomas Flynn, born ~1818 in Ireland, plausibly died between ca. 1860 and ca. 1905 — his lifespan sets this window, not Patrick's. A will or administration naming Patrick Flynn as a son or heir would be the most direct parentage evidence available and the record type most likely to resolve the question outright. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection (1683–1994, collection 1999196) returned personCount 0 from collections_search, making this a browse-only (personCount 0) image search; image group 007936749 covers Schuylkill County probate 1851–1930, fully within this window. If Thomas married in Pennsylvania after emigrating (~1847–1850), a Catholic marriage register from a Schuylkill County parish will record the union and supply the wife's maiden name — Patrick's mother's birth surname, which the census never gives. The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable (personCount 982,415) and covers 1708–1985. The marriage date relative to Patrick's birth (~1845) corroborates Thomas as father, but this record alone does not place Patrick in the household — items 1 and 2 carry that link. If Thomas married in Ireland before emigrating, this Pennsylvania search will return nothing and Irish Catholic registers would be the follow-on target.

Broader search of the Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415) for Thomas Flynn's children: baptisms of Patrick's siblings naming both parents are direct parentage evidence for the siblings and strongly corroborate the same parentage for Patrick. The search also covers Patrick's own post-immigration confirmation, any burial entries for Thomas or his wife, and records naming him as godparent. Loc_001 notes that Catholic parishes in Schuylkill County fell under the Diocese of Philadelphia until 1875 (and the Diocese of Allentown from 1961); sacramental registers survive at the parish or diocesan level, and some are digitized in this collection.

Thomas Flynn emigrated from Ireland and would have filed for naturalization in Schuylkill County after 1849. Image group 007936750 (Schuylkill County Naturalization Records, 1849–1915) is browse-only (personCount 0). Declarations of intention and petitions name the declarant's country and sometimes county or parish of origin, date of arrival, and age. If Thomas's papers survive, they may narrow the Irish county of origin — enabling a future search of Irish Catholic parish registers for Patrick's baptism, where both parents would be named. A stated father's name on Patrick's marriage certificate corroborates Thomas Flynn as his father (secondary evidence — informant is typically the parties themselves); a stated mother's name identifies Patrick's mother if items 1–2 and 4–5 have not already done so. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

entry.rationale: Thomas Flynn (born ~1818 Ireland, candidate father) could plausibly have died any time from the 1860s through the 1890s; Thomas's lifespan sets this window. The localities entry (loc_001) confirms the Schuylkill County Register of Wills holds probate records from 1811 and identifies them as a primary parentage source naming heirs. A will or estate administration naming Patrick Flynn as a son or heir is DIRECT parentage evidence that would advance the conclusion from Probable to Proved. Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994 (collection 1999196) is browse-only (personCount 0) — the search must browse the alphabetical docket images rather than using a name search. S4 in the project tree cites Schuylkill County Probate Records but no assertion has been extracted from it; this is the first search of that source for Thomas Flynn specifically.

Thomas Flynn's marriage to Patrick's mother has not been searched. A dedicated parentage-plan item for the candidate parents' marriage is required: it confirms the couple as a unit and — critically — supplies the mother's maiden name, which neither the 1850 nor the 1860 census records (which do not record relationships or the wife's pre-marriage name). The marriage date relative to Patrick's ~1845 birth also corroborates Thomas as the father, though the marriage record alone does not prove Patrick is their child. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable; search on surname Flynn with given Thomas. The localities entry (loc_001) notes Schuylkill County's Roman Catholic parishes were under the Diocese of Philadelphia; the same collection covers multiple denominations. Account for spelling variants: Flyn, Flinn, Flynne.

Patrick Flynn was born ~1845 in Ireland, so his own baptism is in Ireland (birth parish unknown); no Pennsylvania baptism for Patrick exists to find. However, siblings born after the Flynn family immigrated to Schuylkill County may have been baptized there. A baptism record naming Thomas Flynn and his wife as parents is DIRECT parentage evidence for that child — and the same parents named on a sibling's baptism corroborate the family unit around Patrick. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable; search parent surname Flynn, given Thomas, across 1843-1875. The mother's given name from pli_007 should be added to this search once known. Search also for any child with surname Flynn in the same household cluster. Account for spelling variants: Flyn, Flinn, Flynne.

Patrick Flynn's own marriage record has not been searched and may name his parents directly — either in the body of a church marriage register or on a civil license application. This is a FAN item: the marriage record is not about the parentage event itself but is a life-event record that routinely names the groom's parents. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable; search on surname Flynn with given Patrick across 1865-1900. If the record names Thomas Flynn as Patrick's father, it constitutes a second secondary-informant statement corroborating the death certificate (assertion a_013), both distinct from the census inferences. The informant (likely Patrick himself) is closer to the parentage event than the son-in-law who completed the death certificate.

The 1870 census has not been searched — an explicit gap in the proof summary. Thomas Flynn (~52) and Patrick Flynn (~25) may appear in the same or adjoining Schuylkill County households. United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Searching both Thomas and Patrick separately. If Thomas's 1870 household includes a wife and other children not yet known to the project, those persons become the next FAN layer. If Patrick appears nearby, continued community ties support the family connection. The 1870 census records occupation and birthplace (Ireland expected for both), providing corroborating data and leads for the wife's name obtained from pli_007.

The 1880 census has not been searched — an explicit gap in the proof summary — and is the FIRST federal census to record each person's relationship to the head of household. Thomas Flynn (~62) may still be alive; any children remaining in his household would appear with an explicit relationship designation (son, daughter) — direct relationship evidence for those individuals, corroborating the family structure that the 1850 and 1860 censuses could only support by inference. Patrick (~35) is likely in his own household by 1880; his entry would also carry the relationship column for his own children, expanding the known FAN cluster. United States Census, 1880 (collection 1417683) is name-searchable.

The 1900 census has not been searched — an explicit gap in the proof summary. Patrick Flynn (~55) should appear in Schuylkill County. The 1900 census records both parents' birthplaces (both expected to be Ireland) and years of immigration — data points that corroborate the Irish origin shared with Thomas Flynn and that may help distinguish this Patrick from others. Patrick's household identifies his wife and children by name, expanding the FAN cluster and confirming the identity of informant James Brown (son-in-law on the 1908 death certificate). United States Census, 1900 (collection 1325221) is name-searchable.

The 1850 and 1860 census indexed entries for Thomas Flynn's household were searched (log_001, log_004), but only Thomas and Patrick were extracted as assertions. The full household page images have not been browsed for additional members. This is a FAN item: browse the images at dwellings 84 (1850) and 112 (1860) to record (a) Thomas's wife by name — she appears in the household but was not extracted; (b) any other children in the household by name and age; and (c) the neighboring families on the same census page, who constitute the immediate community FAN cluster and may share the Flynn family's Irish parish of origin. The wife's name unlocks searches in pli_008 and pli_007. This is a browse step on already-located images, not a new name search.

Schuylkill County deed books record Thomas Flynn as grantor or grantee in any real property transactions. Land deeds supply FAN names in three ways: (a) the boundary recital names adjoining landowners — neighbors by definition; (b) attesting witnesses are typically neighbors or associates; and (c) a deed of partition or a conveyance recording the distribution of Thomas's estate would name his heirs, providing parentage evidence comparable to a will. The localities entry (loc_001) identifies the Register of Wills as the primary parentage source; the Recorder of Deeds is the secondary FAN route if probate yields no will. Deed books for Schuylkill County are held at the county courthouse; some volumes may be available as browse images through the FamilySearch Catalog. This item is a fallback if pli_006 (probate) finds no will or estate administration for Thomas Flynn.

Finally, a surname-broad search for any Bankston appearing in those same marriage registers as a party or witness helps locate the family's geographic cluster within the split parish, which is indirect but useful evidence if Silas's own entry proves elusive.

The next step is to run the name-indexed searches of the East and West Feliciana Parish marriage records on FamilySearch.

response.objective: Determine why Michael Sheahan relocated to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882

openQuestions.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?

questionStatuses.nextStep: research-plan

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

entry.rationale: The 1880 US Census (collection 1417683, name-searchable) is the single most critical record: taken two years before Michael's unsourced 1882 Schuylkill County residence fact (F2), it will reveal either that he was already in Schuylkill County or exactly where he was living immediately before the recorded move. The 1880 census also reports occupation for every household member — if Michael is already listed as a miner in 1880, the coal-mining motivation is corroborated before the 1882 date in the tree; if he is elsewhere with a different occupation, the shift to mining becomes part of the story. Neighbors listed on the same page are a supplemental FAN resource. Variant spellings — Sheehan, Shehan, Shahan — should all be tried.

The 1870 US Census (collection 1438024, name-searchable) corresponds to tree fact F1, which records Michael in Pennsylvania in 1870 but gives no county. Finding his specific county and occupation at that date establishes the pre-move baseline: was he already a miner elsewhere in Pennsylvania before his sibling Patrick moved to Schuylkill County in 1875, or did he enter the anthracite mining trade only after arriving in Schuylkill County? The answer distinguishes 'moved for mining work already underway' from 'moved and then became a miner.' Patrick Sheahan should also be searched at this date to establish where both brothers were before the 1875 land purchase.

The 1900 US Census (collection 1325221, name-searchable) uniquely asked for year of immigration and years in the United States for foreign-born residents. The Irish surname Sheahan strongly suggests immigrant origin; if Michael was born in Ireland, the 1900 schedule will establish when he arrived in America — showing whether he emigrated directly to Schuylkill County or arrived elsewhere first, which is central to understanding his migration path. The 1900 census also shows 18 years of post-move settlement: continued occupation as miner, residence stability, and household composition. Occupation continuity from 1882 to 1900 would strengthen the coal-mining motivation claim.

The Schuylkill County Naturalization Records 1849-1915 (image group 007936750, browse-only (personCount 0)) are not name-indexed and must be browsed image by image — confirmed by the locality guide's note that some naturalization films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only. If Michael was a foreign-born immigrant, his declaration of intent or final papers would state his country and county of birth and often his year of US arrival, supplying direct evidence about the migration path. An Irish-born coal miner naturalizing in Schuylkill County during the 1880s-1890s follows a well-documented pattern; the record would also link him to a specific court date and potentially a colliery employer who served as a witness.

The Pennsylvania Schuylkill County Church Records collection (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH, name-searchable, personCount 982,415) covers 1842-1895 and spans Michael's arrival period. Michael's Irish surname and miner occupation in the anthracite region strongly suggest Roman Catholic affiliation; the locality guide confirms that RC parishes in Schuylkill County were under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875). Catholic registers in the anthracite coal region frequently recorded a parishioner's place of origin in Ireland — not just a country but often the townland or civil parish — which would identify the chain-migration path independent of what census or naturalization records state. Finding a sacramental entry for Michael shortly after 1882 would also corroborate his arrival date.

FAN item targeting Patrick Sheahan's settlement context. Patrick (Michael's sibling, I2) purchased land in Schuylkill County in 1875, documented in S1 (Deed Book 42, p. 118, seven years before Michael's 1882 arrival). The Schuylkill County Deed Records 1815-1900 (image group 007936752, 22% searchable) should be searched for any additional transactions in Patrick's name — and for Michael's name after 1882 — to determine whether the brothers acquired adjacent or nearby lots, a pattern typical of Irish chain migration in the Pennsylvania coal region. The locality guide notes that much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers, so a deed in Michael's own name would be significant. Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.

If the census and church searches leave the arrival date uncertain, a directory sequence spanning several years would resolve it. items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

entry.rationale: S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates, cert. no. 4521, 12 March 1908) is already sourced in the tree for Patrick's death, but no assertions about his parents' names have been extracted for q_001. Pennsylvania's 1906 statewide death registration required informants to name the decedent's father and mother; this single record could directly name both parents. The informant's relationship to Patrick and their likely knowledge of the mother's maiden name — especially if Thomas had predeceased Patrick — must be assessed, but even secondary information in a death certificate is a significant lead. This is the fastest available path to both parents' names from a record already in hand.

S2 (1860 U.S. Federal Census, Schuylkill Co., dwelling 112) is cited in the tree for the ParentChild relationship R1, but its household assertions — including the presence and identity of Patrick's mother and any siblings — have not been extracted for q_001. United States Census, 1860 (collection 1473181) is name-searchable. Thomas (~42) and Patrick (~15) should appear; the mother, if living, would be enumerated alongside them, giving her name and approximate age. Search Flynn and variant Flinn.

United States Census, 1870 (collection 1438024) is name-searchable. Thomas Flynn (~52) and Patrick (~25) may share a household in Schuylkill County in 1870; if the mother is still living, she would be enumerated with them. A household entry naming Thomas's wife alongside Patrick would provide the mother's name and approximate age, corroborating the parentage link. Search Flynn and variant Flinn.

The 1880 census is the first to record each person's relationship to the household head explicitly, making it the strongest census source for confirming parentage. Thomas (~62) and Patrick (~35) may still share a Schuylkill County household; if so, the relationship field would record Patrick as 'son' — stronger evidence than 1850 co-enumeration alone — and would name Thomas's wife (Patrick's mother) as 'wife.' Search Flynn and variant Flinn.

Thomas Flynn, born ~1818 in Ireland, likely died in Schuylkill County between approximately 1860 and 1895; this date window is set by Thomas's own plausible lifespan, not Patrick's research dates. Mode: **create** — q_001, "Who were the parents of Patrick Flynn (b. ~1845, PA, d. 1908)?"

- No mother is recorded anywhere in the tree
- S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is in the tree sources but is not attached to any person or relationship — identified but not yet searched
- Proof summary ps_001 is at tier "possible" with shortfall "gap"; only the 1850 census has been searched for q_001; post-1860 censuses, probate, church, and vital records are all unsearched

**Plan pl_002 — 10 items:**

- pli_004 — vital_record, Schuylkill County PA, 1908, FamilySearch: S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates, cert. 4521) is in the tree for Patrick's death but parents' names have not been extracted; a 1908 death certificate under the 1906 state registration law names both father and mother — the fastest available path to both parents' names

- pli_006 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1870, FamilySearch: collection 1438024 is name-searchable; Thomas (~52) and Patrick (~25) may share a household, and the mother, if surviving, would be named
- pli_007 — census, Schuylkill County PA, 1880, FamilySearch: collection 1417683 is name-searchable; the 1880 schedule is the first to state each person's relationship to the household head explicitly, making co-residence with Thomas the strongest census evidence for parentage and naming the mother as "wife"
- pli_008 — probate, Schuylkill County PA, 1860-1895, FamilySearch: Thomas born ~1818 likely died within this window (set by his lifespan); S4 (Schuylkill County Probate Records) is in the tree but unattached; Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 and Schuylkill dockets 1851-1930 are both browse-only (personCount 0); a will naming Patrick as son is direct parentage evidence and would name the mother
- pli_009 — church, Schuylkill County PA, 1838-1910, FamilySearch (dedicated parents' marriage item): SYNTH-PA-CHURCH (Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records, 1708-1985) is name-searchable; search for the parents' marriage (supplying the mother's maiden name), siblings' baptisms (naming both parents directly), and Thomas's burial entry (corroborating his death date for the probate search); the parents' marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child — a record placing him in their household is also required

- pli_013 — land (FAN cluster), Schuylkill County PA, 1845-1885, FamilySearch: volume 007936752 (Deed Records 1815-1900) is 22% indexed; deed boundary recitals name adjoining landowners (frequently kin) and deed witnesses are often associates — a second Flynn alongside Thomas is a FAN lead whose own records may name Patrick's mother; required FAN item for a parentage question

The plan addresses the question of who Patrick Flynn's parents were. He died in March 1908 in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, and his father Thomas Flynn is already in the family tree based on census co-residence — but no mother has been found and the connection to Thomas rests only on indirect evidence so far. The plan begins with Patrick's own 1908 death certificate, which is already on file and should name both his father and mother directly; that is the single fastest step. From there the plan works through the 1860, 1870, and 1880 federal census records to trace the household and find the mother enumerated alongside Thomas and Patrick — particularly the 1880 census, which for the first time explicitly states each person's relationship to the head of the household. If Thomas left a will in Schuylkill County (probable given his age and the family's long residence there), that probate record could name Patrick as a son outright and name the mother as Thomas's wife. Alongside that, the plan searches the indexed Catholic parish register collection for the county, looking for the parents' marriage record (which would give the mother's maiden name), baptism records of Patrick's siblings (which would name both parents), and Thomas's burial entry; a browse-only image volume of the same parish records acts as a fallback if the index misses anything. Thomas's naturalization papers are also planned — Irish-immigrant naturalization declarations from this era often name the applicant's county of origin in Ireland and his family, which would open the door to searching Irish church records later. A final search of Schuylkill County deed records looks at the family's neighbors and associates (the people most likely to be kin) for other Flynns who might identify the mother through their own records.

The next step is to retrieve and read Patrick's 1908 death certificate, then work through the census and probate searches in sequence on FamilySearch.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.
